##### DAGs and SWIGs

NPSEMs are characterized using the set of conditional indpendencies that hold among their random variables. It is possible to deduce these using the structural equations themselves —- we can check whether two variables are (conditionally) independent by checking whether both are a function of the same error term. It turns out that queries like this are much simpler to answer through a graphical representation of the NPSEM than through the NPSEM itself, however. Directed acyclic graphs allow the efficient communication of conditional independence assumptions that define NPSEMs.

A causal directed acyclic graph (DAG) (@fig-fully-connected-dag) is a graph whose nodes represent the variables in an NPSEM (@eq-fully-connected-dag). Directed edges point from the arguments to the result of each structural equation.

{{< include fig-fully-connected-dag.qmd >}}

A single-world intervention graph (SWIG) (@fig-fully-connected-swig) is a DAG whose nodes represent the variables in the interventional data model included in a causal model (@eq-fully-connected-swig). Directed edges point from the arguments to the result of each structural equation.

{{< include fig-fully-connected-swig.qmd >}}

DAGs and SWIGs are useful because they encode statistical relationships among the variables in an NPSEM through a set of graphical rules called [d-separation](#sec-d-separation). Two variables in an NPSEM are (conditionally) independent if they are (conditionally) [d-separated](#sec-d-separation) in the causal DAG representing the NPSEM.
